Mobile robots that map tunnels, mines and long corridors lose their LiDAR odometry when the scene stops constraining a direction of motion. In a corridor with smooth walls the motion along the axis is unobserved, and a camera-based estimator has to carry that direction. Switching methods such as Switch-SLAM choose between LiDAR and visual odometry with one eigenvalue test on the whole registration Hessian, in which rotation (radians) and translation (metres) share one scale.

This work builds a LiDAR-visual-inertial odometry front end on A-LOAM and VINS-Mono that judges the two parts separately. The Schur complements of the A-LOAM Hessian give a rotation block (channel R) and a translation block (channel T), and the translation block sets a per-direction weight between the LiDAR and the VINS-Mono increments. A third channel, the additional T, is computed from the raw keyframe points: the orientation tensor of the surface normals and edge directions bounds the translation information direction by direction, and the same normals correct the heading. Versions F20 to F24 added a VINS-Mono trust check, an anchored hand-over and a guard on A-LOAM's initial guess. The final version, F35, also takes the decision rule of Switch-SLAM into the LiDAR matching: VINS-Mono's motion seeds A-LOAM's scan-to-map step only when the scan is degenerate.

Accuracy is measured as the absolute trajectory error (ATE): the root-mean-square distance in metres between the estimated and the true positions after the two paths have been fitted to each other. Without loop closure and with frozen settings, F35 gave an ATE of 0.54 m on SubT-MRS Multi Floor and 2.10 m on Long Corridor, against 1.61 m and 2.42 m published for Switch-SLAM, and 0.29 m on a simulated farm route against 0.38 m. It had a lower mean error than VINS-Mono alone and than A-LOAM alone on all six sequences, by 39 to 98 %, but on Cave02 (6.23 m) it was above an earlier version (4.4 m). With one to three live runs per sequence, only the GEODE comparison with VINS-Mono alone is significant (p = 0.008), and every sequence was used during development, so the results are not a held-out test.<pb/>

Autonomous mobile robots now carry material in factories and warehouses, inspect tunnels and mines, and survey places where a person should not go. Each of these jobs needs the robot to know where it is and what its surroundings look like, which is the problem of simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) [1]. A robot that does SLAM well can plan a path, return to a charging point and leave behind a map that people can use. A robot that does it badly drifts, and in a long tunnel a few degrees of heading error become several metres of position error.

Three sensors are common on such robots. A 3D LiDAR measures the geometry of the scene directly and at metric scale, so LiDAR odometry such as LOAM [2] and its successors [3]-[5] is accurate wherever the scene has enough structure. A camera sees texture, and an inertial measurement unit (IMU) measures angular rate and acceleration; visual-inertial odometry (VIO) such as VINS-Mono [6] combines the two. The sensors fail in different places. The LiDAR fails where the geometry repeats itself, and the camera fails in the dark, on bare walls and during fast rotation. The DARPA Subterranean Challenge showed how often both happen underground [7].

A LiDAR odometry estimates the motion between scans by registering the new scan to a map, usually by Gauss-Newton or Levenberg-Marquardt minimisation of point-to-plane and point-to-line distances. The registration Hessian H (6 x 6, three rotation and three translation directions) says how strongly the scan constrains each direction. When the walls of a corridor are smooth and parallel, every plane normal is perpendicular to the corridor axis, so a shift along the axis does not change any residual and H has a near-zero eigenvalue in that direction. The solver still returns an answer, but along that direction it is determined by noise and by the initial guess. Zhang, Kaess and Singh called this degeneracy and proposed to detect it from the eigenvalues of H [8].

Figure 1.1 shows this in a corridor. The robot moves from position 1 to position 2, and the two scans look alike, because each shows only two flat walls. The walls fix where the robot is across the corridor, but a scan taken further along the corridor looks the same, so it does not say how far the robot has moved.
Figure 1.1: LiDAR degeneracy in a corridor (schematic): the scans at positions 1 and 2 look the same, so the motion along the corridor is not constrained

The effect is large on real data. In this work A-LOAM [9], run on its own, gave an absolute trajectory error (ATE) of 15.8 m on the 579 m SubT-MRS Long Corridor sequence and 66 m on the 695 m Corridor02 sequence, against 0.5 to 2.1 m for the fused estimates reported later. In the Multi Floor sequence, where a legged robot climbs stairs between floors, A-LOAM alone gave 26.4 m.

Every error in this report is given as the absolute trajectory error, so it helps to say what that is. At each moment of a run the estimator reports a position, and the dataset (or the simulator) gives the true position at the same moment. The absolute trajectory error is the typical distance between the two, in metres, after the estimated path has been laid over the true path as closely as it will fit (Figure 4.3 and Section 4.7). A value of 2.1 m on a path of 579 m means that the estimate is usually about 2 m from the truth, which is 0.4 % of the distance travelled. Smaller is better.

A monocular VIO such as VINS-Mono [6] tracks image features and integrates the IMU between frames. It does not depend on the geometry of the scene, so it keeps working in a corridor, but its scale is observable only through the accelerometer and it drifts slowly in heading. It also needs texture and parallax: a pure in-place rotation gives no parallax, and a dark or featureless wall gives no features. On the sequences of this work VINS-Mono alone gave 1.28 m on Multi Floor, 5.81 m on Long Corridor, 4.03 m on Corridor02 and 10.25 m on Cave02, and on the GEODE stairs sequence it lost track repeatedly and reached 150 to 270 m. The LiDAR is the better sensor where the geometry is rich, and the VIO is the better sensor along a degenerate direction.

Switch-SLAM [10] runs LiDAR-inertial and visual-inertial odometry side by side and switches the initial pose of the LiDAR odometry to the visual estimate when it detects LiDAR degeneracy. The detector compares the eigenvalues of the registration Hessian with a threshold derived from the semicircle law of random matrices. Two features of this design leave room for improvement. The test is applied to the whole Hessian, in which rotation is measured in radians and translation in metres, so a rotation problem can be hidden by the larger translation numbers and the reverse. The decision is also all or nothing: the whole pose comes from one source, although in a corridor only one translation direction is lost and the other five are still well constrained by the LiDAR. The detector trusts the solver's own Hessian, and a solver that converges to a wrong minimum can report a confident Hessian.

To build a LiDAR-inertial-visual odometry that detects LiDAR degeneracy separately for rotation and translation, using the Schur complements of the registration Hessian, adds a check computed from the raw scan geometry that does not depend on the solver, and uses both to weight the LiDAR and VIO motion direction by direction instead of switching between them.

To separate the rotation and translation information of the A-LOAM registration Hessian with Schur complements (channels R and T) and use the translation block to weight the LiDAR and VINS-Mono increments per direction.

To add an independent channel from the raw keyframe geometry, the orientation tensor of surface normals and edges, that checks the translation information and corrects the heading (the additional T channel).

To choose the scan-to-map initial guess of A-LOAM from the degeneracy status given by the rules of Switch-SLAM (version F35, the final version), with three safeguards: a VIO-trust check, an anchored hand-over and a guard on the mapping guess.
To implement the method live in ROS on A-LOAM and VINS-Mono and test it on the SubT-MRS Multi Floor and Long Corridor sequences, Corridor02, Cave02, GEODE stairs and a Gazebo farm simulation.
To compare the final version with VINS-Mono alone, A-LOAM alone and the published Switch-SLAM results on Farm, Multi Floor and Long Corridor, with frozen settings and without loop closure.<pb/>

This chapter reviews how degeneracy has been detected from the registration Hessian, how rotation and translation have been separated, how surface-normal statistics have been used as a geometry-based measure, and how LiDAR, visual and inertial odometry have been combined in degenerate scenes.
2.2 Degeneracy detection from the registration Hessian

Gelfand et al. [11] analysed the stability of point-to-plane ICP through the eigenvectors of the 6 x 6 covariance of the constraint and sampled points so that weak directions are covered. Zhang, Kaess and Singh [8] defined a degeneracy factor as the smallest eigenvalue of the Hessian and projected the solution update onto the well-constrained subspace (solution remapping). Their threshold is a constant chosen per sensor setup. Hinduja et al. [12] carried the same idea into a factor graph by adding only the constrained directions of a registration factor, and applied it to underwater SLAM.

Later work made the test less ad hoc. Hatleskog and Alexis [13] propagated the point noise into the eigenvalues and decided degeneracy with a probabilistic test instead of a fixed threshold. Nubert et al. [14] learned localizability from simulated data. X-ICP [15] computed localizability per direction from the contribution of each point and constrained the optimisation in the weak directions, and a field study [16] compared detection and mitigation strategies of this kind on real data from several robots.

The eigenvalues of the full Hessian mix two units. A rotation eigenvalue scales with the square of the range of the points, a translation eigenvalue does not, so a threshold that suits one is wrong for the other. DCReg [17] separates the two with Schur complements: the rotation block is the rotation information left after the translation has been estimated, and the reverse. On the SubT-MRS Cave02 and GEODE stairs sequences, where rotation and translation are strongly coupled, it reported localisation errors of a few centimetres where minimum-eigenvalue detection failed. DCReg is a registration method; it does not fuse a second sensor.

The distribution of the surface normals of a scan describes which directions the scene can constrain, without reference to any solver. The Bingham distribution [18] is the standard model for axial data such as normals, and its sufficient statistic is the second-moment orientation tensor T = (1/n) sum n n<sup>T</sup> [19]. Orientation tensors of second and fourth order are also used to describe fibre orientation in composites [20]. In LiDAR odometry, LF-GICP [21] builds a planarity-weighted normal tensor of the map and uses its smallest eigenvalue to gate a reweighting of the registration, arguing that the Gauss-Newton Hessian can hide degeneracy. The orientation tensor as a solver-independent degeneracy measure is therefore prior art; LF-GICP is LiDAR-only and does not use the tensor to correct heading.

Tightly coupled LiDAR-inertial odometries such as LIO-SAM [4] and FAST-LIO2 [5] use the IMU to bridge short degenerate stretches, but do not use a camera. LVI-SAM [22] couples a visual-inertial and a LiDAR-inertial subsystem; the visual system gives the initial guess of the LiDAR scan matching, and the LiDAR depth helps the visual features. RELEAD [23] constrains the LiDAR optimisation in non-localizable directions and fuses it with VIO in a graph. ORB-SLAM3 [24] is a feature-based visual-inertial SLAM with maps and relocalisation, but it has no LiDAR. Switch-SLAM [10], described in Section 1.4, is the closest system to this work. Its status rule (Section 4.5) is reused in the final version, and its published results (Table II of that paper, without loop closure) are the targets used in Chapter 5.

SubT-MRS [25] provides LiDAR, camera and IMU data from legged, wheeled and handheld platforms in tunnels, caves, corridors and stairwells, with ground-truth trajectories; its Multi Floor and Long Corridor sequences are used by Switch-SLAM. GEODE [26] provides several LiDAR types in degenerate scenes, including a stairwell with a map-based ground truth. Both are used in this work, together with a Gazebo [27] farm world; Switch-SLAM also evaluated its method on simulated Gazebo scenes, including a farm.

Three points come out of the review. Rotation and translation degeneracy have different causes and units and are better judged separately, and the Schur complement is a clean way to do it . The methods that separate them work on the LiDAR alone and rely on the solver's own Hessian. The fusion systems that add a camera, switch the whole pose or the initial guess and do not weight directions. No system found in this review combines Schur-separated channels with an independent check from the raw geometry inside a LiDAR-visual-inertial fusion. That combination is the subject of this work.<pb/>

The work was done in the order of Figure 3.1. After a first-generation switching node and a study of 15 detection rules (Section 5.2), the fusion channels were designed and their constants frozen on recorded runs. Live runs then exposed failures that replays had not shown; each was fixed by a small, testable change (F20 to F24), and F35 changed only A-LOAM's initial guess. Every live test had a pass rule written before it was run, and every run is reported. A version name such as F24 stands for one fixed set of settings of the fusion node; Table 4.3 lists them and Section 5.1 gives a short key.

The fusion splits the work by direction (Figure 3.2). For every LiDAR scan the node receives A-LOAM's scan-to-map pose and Hessian and the pose of VINS-Mono. Rotation comes from VINS-Mono. Translation comes from the LiDAR along the directions the scan constrains and from VINS-Mono along the others. Where VINS-Mono is unusable (warm-up, loss, or a failed trust check), the LiDAR carries the whole step. The node forms the LiDAR increment (rotation vector φ<sub>L</sub>, translation Δt<sub>L</sub>) and the VINS increment (φ<sub>V</sub>, Δt<sub>V</sub>) since the previous scan and blends them with two 3 x 3 weights:

The fused pose is the previous fused pose composed with this increment. W = 0 means the VIO carries a direction, W = I means the LiDAR carries it. For the first 20 s after VINS-Mono starts (T<sub>warm</sub>) the output is LiDAR only, because a monocular VIO needs time to settle its scale; the same warm-up is repeated after VINS-Mono is lost (mode VO_FAIL: no message, a jump above 1 m or 0.5 rad, or a restart). The loop is closed: the fused pose, moved forward by a step chosen as in Section 4.5, is A-LOAM's initial guess for the next scan. A-LOAM here has no IMU of its own; inertial information reaches the LiDAR side only through VINS-Mono's pose.

3.3 Schur decomposition of the registration Hessian
The A-LOAM Hessian is partitioned into rotation (R) and translation (t) blocks, with rotation in radians and translation in metres:
The Schur complements give the information about one part after the other part has been estimated from the same data:

S<sub>tt</sub> is the translation information that is left once the scan's rotation is free, and S<sub>RR</sub> the reverse. Each is a 3 x 3 matrix in one unit, so its eigenvalues can be compared within the block. In a corridor S<sub>tt</sub> has one small eigenvalue along the axis and two large ones across it.
The translation block is turned into a weight by treating the LiDAR increment as a measurement with information c<sub>T</sub> S<sub>tt</sub> and the VIO increment as a prior with information γ I:
W<sub>t</sub> = (c<sub>T</sub> S<sub>tt</sub> + γ I)<sup>-1</sup> c<sub>T</sub> S<sub>tt</sub>(3.6)

Along an eigenvector of S<sub>tt</sub> with eigenvalue λ the weight is c<sub>T</sub>λ / (c<sub>T</sub>λ + γ): close to 1 where the scene constrains the motion and close to 0 along a degenerate axis. There is no switching threshold; the condition-number gate of earlier versions is disabled (KAPPA_TH = 10<sup>9</sup>). The scale c<sub>T</sub> = 0.03 was chosen once on Multi Floor recordings (smallest mean ATE, middle of the plateau) and has not been changed since. γ = 1 normally; Section 4.4 describes when it changes.
3.5 Channel R: rotation block and rotation check

With A-LOAM the VINS-Mono rotation was better than the LiDAR rotation on most sequences: an active rotation weight (c<sub>R</sub> > 0) improved Long Corridor in early replays, while on Multi Floor, Corridor02 and Cave02 the VIO rotation gave the lower error, and an open-loop replay of the F35 logs with c<sub>R</sub> from 10<sup>-5</sup> to 3 x 10<sup>-3</sup> gave Cave02 2.4 m higher at every setting (Table 5.13). In normal operation c<sub>R</sub> = 0, the rotation comes from the VIO and S<sub>RR</sub> is monitored. A rotation check compares the VIO and LiDAR rotations over 2 s and 10 s windows; when they disagree by more than 0.402 rad and 0.585 rad (the largest values on 19 Multi Floor recordings), the LiDAR rotation carries the step with W<sub>R</sub> = (S<sub>RR</sub> + 10<sup>-3</sup> I)<sup>-1</sup> S<sub>RR</sub>. The check closed on no fused scan of four sequences and on 3.6 % of those of GEODE, so it acts as a safeguard for strong disagreement.
3.6 Additional T channel: the orientation tensor

For each LiDAR keyframe the 12 nearest neighbours of every point are found and their covariance is decomposed (eigenvalues λ<sub>1</sub> ≤ λ<sub>2</sub> ≤ λ<sub>3</sub>). A point is planar when (λ<sub>2</sub> - λ<sub>1</sub>)/λ<sub>3</sub> > 0.5, with normal n, and linear when (λ<sub>3</sub> - λ<sub>2</sub>)/λ<sub>3</sub> > 0.5, with direction d. A plane constrains translation along its normal; an edge constrains translation in the plane perpendicular to its direction. The geometric orientation tensor counts both:
G = ( Σ<sub>planar</sub> n n<sup>T</sup> + ½ Σ<sub>linear</sub> (I - d d<sup>T</sup>) ) / (n<sub>p</sub> + n<sub>l</sub>)(3.7)

G has trace 1 and uses no correspondences, no solver state and no threshold. Between keyframes it is rotated into the current LiDAR frame. Planar normals alone understate the support that A-LOAM has from edge features such as door frames and pipes, so edge directions are included; rules built on planar normals alone gave corridor errors 0.26 to 1.0 m higher in replay.

The tensor is scaled to the same total information as the solver, B = tr(H<sub>tt</sub>) G, and combined with A = S<sub>tt</sub> by a basis-free matrix rule. Several rules were compared by replay on clean data and under injected faults (Section 5.9). The final version uses the generalised maximum:
S'<sub>tt</sub> = B<sup>½</sup> max(M, I) B<sup>½</sup>,   M = B<sup>-½</sup> A B<sup>-½</sup>(3.8)

where max(M, I) raises every generalised eigenvalue below 1 to 1. Along each direction the combined information is the larger of what the solver and the raw geometry support, and S'<sub>tt</sub> replaces S<sub>tt</sub> in Equation 3.6. F20 used the opposite rule (the minimum, a fail-safe cap). The maximum was chosen in a pre-registered comparison because it scored best over the clean and fault cells and on a farm bag that the comparison had not used; protection against a solver that is confident but wrong comes from the VIO-trust check of Section 4.4.

The second read-out of the normals corrects heading, which VINS-Mono cannot observe and which dominates the error in long corridors. The near-vertical planar normals of a keyframe are levelled with the VIO gravity direction, and their horizontal directions form an axial histogram h(θ) (0.5° bins over 180°). The heading error is the shift, searched over ±15°, that best aligns h(θ) with a reference histogram learned in the world frame; it passes through a Kalman update and is applied at no more than 0.25° per scan. It switches itself off when the structure is not distinct (a null-model test against random directions, a unique correlation peak, a chi-square gate and a drift gate). This structure-anchored heading (SAH) depends on the even-order orientation tensors of the same normals; the fourth order matters, because with two equally strong perpendicular wall families the second-order tensor is isotropic and carries no heading information.<pb/>

4.4 Safeguards added after the live tests

VIO-trust check (F21). For every scan the ratio of VINS and LiDAR path lengths over 10 s windows inside one VINS segment is formed, and r is the RMS of ln(|ΔtV|/|ΔtL|). While r stays at or below 0.157 (and a fast 5 s version at or below 0.277), γ = 1 in Equation 3.6; otherwise γ = 0 and the LiDAR carries the step. Both references, and the guard constant below, were set from six Multi Floor calibration replays. A LiDAR guard works the other way: while the VINS is trusted, a LiDAR path that runs more than 4.325 m ahead of the VINS path within 2 s marks the LiDAR step as failed.

Anchored hand-over (F22, F23). In the live Long Corridor runs of F20 the fused heading jumped by 6 to 7° at the first fused scan: the warm-up had already integrated a fast turn with the LiDAR rotation, and VINS-Mono, which lagged by about 5°, added its catch-up of the same turn. At every entry into the fused mode the rotation is now reset to
R<sub>f</sub> = R<sub>off</sub> R<sub>vL</sub>,   R<sub>off</sub> = mean<sub>k</sub> ( R<sub>A,k</sub> R<sub>vL,k</sub><sup>T</sup> )(4.1)

where R<sub>vL</sub> is the LiDAR orientation predicted by VINS-Mono, R<sub>A,k</sub> the A-LOAM orientation at warm-up scan k, and the mean is a robust chordal mean over all warm-up scans of the current VINS segment. VINS-Mono then continues from a reference consistent with itself, so its catch-up removes the transient instead of adding it.

Mapping-guess guard (F24). In a live farm run of F23 the error reached 5.3 m in the first 18 s, while VINS-Mono was failing. The likely cause, not proven by that single run, is that VINS steps of 1 to 3 m were passed into A-LOAM's initial guess and A-LOAM's odometry followed them. In F24 a VINS step counts as usable for the guess only when the previous mode was not VO_FAIL and the step is within the jump limits (1 m, 0.5 rad). The fused output itself is unchanged by this rule.
4.5 Scan-to-map guess from the degeneracy status (F35)

Up to F24 the guess for A-LOAM's scan-to-map matching was the last fused pose moved by the VINS-Mono step wherever that step was usable, and the last fused pose with no motion otherwise. On Cave02 and GEODE the no-motion guess was used on 13.5 % and 78 % of the scans, while VINS-Mono was starting or failing, and where the scan is well constrained the VINS step only adds VINS-Mono's noise to a match that does not need it.

F35 chooses the guess with the status rule of Switch-SLAM [10]. The six eigenvalues of H are computed and the three smallest, scaled to unit length, are compared with the published thresholds [0.12, 0.27, 0.48]; the scan is degenerate if any of them is below its threshold. The flags of the last five scans form a status queue. With Δ<sub>L</sub> the A-LOAM scan-to-scan increment and Δ<sub>V</sub> the VINS-Mono increment, the step added to the last fused pose is
Δ<sub>g</sub> = Δ<sub>L</sub> (none flagged),   w Δ<sub>L</sub> + (1 - w) Δ<sub>V</sub> (mixed),   Δ<sub>V</sub> (all flagged)(4.2)

with w = min(1, √3 λ̄<sub>1</sub>) from the smallest scaled eigenvalue (Eq. 13 of Switch-SLAM). A VINS step that fails the F24 guard counts as absent. Only A-LOAM's starting point changes; the output is still the fusion of Equations 3.1 and 3.2. The output is not switched or remapped as in Switch-SLAM: that structure, with A-LOAM's pose as the output and our channels as the detector, was tested as F30 to F34; the weighted fusion was lower on every sequence they were run on (Table 5.13).

A variant, F26, drives the same queue with channels R, T and the additional T instead of the published thresholds. It put the VINS step into the guess on 73 % of the Long Corridor scans (F35: 2 %). On the four sequences with runs the reading rule written beforehand gave no change against F35: Corridor02 was higher (2.82 against 1.99 m) and the others were inconclusive. F35 remains the final version. Table 5.5 sets F26 and F35 side by side on every sequence.

Every result in Chapter 5 answers the same question: how far is the estimated path from the true path? The true path, the ground truth, comes from the dataset or, in the simulation, from the Gazebo model pose. At each scan time the estimator gives a position pi and the ground truth gives a position gi. The two are written in different coordinate frames, and the estimator starts from an arbitrary origin, so the estimated path is first fitted to the true one by a single rotation and shift (Figure 4.3). The distance that remains at each scan is the error ei. The ATE is the root mean square of these distances, a typical error in metres, and the maximum error is the largest single distance. The definition is given formally below, and Table 4.5 shows how each number in Chapter 5 is read.
Figure 4.3: Computing the ATE (schematic): the estimated path is fitted to the ground truth, and the distances that remain give the error

The accuracy measure is the absolute trajectory error [29]. The estimated positions p<sub>i</sub> are aligned to the ground truth g<sub>i</sub> by the rigid transformation (R, t) that minimises the squared error, without scale (Umeyama [30]), over the full span of the run, and
ATE = ( (1/N) Σ<sub>i</sub> || R p<sub>i</sub> + t - g<sub>i</sub> ||<sup>2</sup> )<sup>½</sup>(4.3)

The maximum of ||R p<sub>i</sub> + t - g<sub>i</sub>|| is reported beside it, as in Switch-SLAM, and all results are front end only, without loop closure. A replay feeds the logged A-LOAM and VINS-Mono poses of a run through the real fusion node; it is exact for the fusion but open loop, because A-LOAM is not re-seeded. Only live runs are compared with published numbers, and differences below max(0.1 m, 10 %) are treated as ties.

The statistics follow Ganesan et al. [31]: minimum, median, maximum and mean per environment, a success rate (here a run with ATE ≤ 10 m), and a one-sided test of H<sub>0</sub>: M(baseline) = M(proposed) against H<sub>1</sub>: M(baseline) > M(proposed) at 95 %, here the exact Mann-Whitney U test on separate live runs, with the Welch t-test beside it where both groups have two or more runs. With n<sub>1</sub> and n<sub>2</sub> runs the exact test cannot go below p = 1 / C(n<sub>1</sub> + n<sub>2</sub>, n<sub>2</sub>). Cave02 and GEODE were first held out, but the F24 results on them led to F25 to F27, so all six sequences are development data for F35.

5.2 First-generation switching node and the threshold study

Question. Does a switching rule that chooses between LiDAR and visual odometry work, and does better detection of degeneracy give a lower error? Answer. On Multi Floor it does not. The error followed how much control was handed to VINS-Mono, not how well degeneracy was detected, and this led to the per-direction weighting used in the rest of the work.

The old switching node gave 1.39 ± 0.14 m on Multi Floor over three runs, against 1.32 m for VINS-Mono alone. Its logs showed three faults: the LiDAR-only mode used scan-to-scan odometry instead of the scan-to-map result, the VINS and LiDAR world frames (8 to 62° apart) were mixed without a rotation, and the largest error came from the VINS start-up transient.

Fifteen detection rules were then run live, one run each, with only the rule changed in the node (Table 5.2). The labels were the A-LOAM drift terciles in 8 s windows on bags 1 and 2 of Multi Floor, which none of the detectors can see, and each rule was scored by Youden's index J = TPR - FPR. An offline screen had predicted J for every rule beforehand, and 13 of the 15 predictions were within 0.05.
Table 5.2: Threshold study on Multi Floor (one live run per rule)

The best detector was A8, the condition number of the rotational Schur block with a threshold found by Otsu's method [28] (J = 0.479, precision 0.817). The old channel T was checked against a rule set before the runs, which required it to add at least 0.05 to J: combined with the Schur test it gave J of 0.152 (C1) and 0.112 (C2) against 0.247 for A2. The more important finding is shown in Figure 5.1. The ATE did not follow the detection quality; it followed the share of time in which control was handed to VINS-Mono (Spearman correlation -0.95). Rules that flagged almost everything (A7) gave a low error because they used VINS-Mono most of the time, and the lowest error on this sequence came from VINS-Mono alone. On this sequence a switching system cannot be judged by how well it detects degeneracy, and switching throws away LiDAR translation that is still good. This result led directly to the per-direction weighting of Chapter 3.

5.4 Behaviour of the channels in a corridor
Question. What do the channels do inside a corridor run? Answer. Across the corridor the LiDAR carries the motion, with a weight near 0.9. Along the corridor VINS-Mono carries about a third of it.

Figure 5.2 shows the channels during the live Long Corridor run of F35. One to three live runs per sequence. Only the GEODE comparison with VINS-Mono alone is significant at 95 % (p = 0.008), and all six sequences were used in development, so the results are not a held-out test.

Channel T is what makes the fusion work at all (Long Corridor 15.8 m for A-LOAM and 5.81 m for VINS-Mono, 4.53 m with channel T alone), and the heading read-out gave the largest single gain (4.53 to about 2.0 m). The tensor rule on S<sub>tt</sub> comes into play under faults, channel R watches the rotation information (its check engaged on 3.6 % of the GEODE scans), and the safeguards of F21 to F24 each removes one observed failure. The status guess of F35 replaced the no-motion guess used on Cave02 and GEODE and lowered the error there; Corridor02 was higher by about 0.5 m.

The threshold study and the F30 to F34 tests agree that a switching system is judged by how much control of the output pose is handed to VINS-Mono; with A-LOAM, the weighted fusion gave a lower error than the switch-and-remap structure on every sequence it was tested on.

F35 has one to three live runs per sequence, and its three GEODE runs spread over 3.1 m. All six sequences were used during development, so the F35 results are development results and a held-out sequence is the next test. On Cave02 the final version gave 6.23 m against 4.4 m for the earlier F8 and F16 versions; the reason for the difference has not yet been identified.<pb/>

A LiDAR-visual-inertial odometry was built on A-LOAM and VINS-Mono in which LiDAR degeneracy is judged in three channels that set per-direction weights between the LiDAR and VIO motion, and F35, which also chooses A-LOAM's initial guess by Switch-SLAM's degeneracy status, was selected as the final version. The main findings are:

Weighting translation by the Schur block S<sub>tt</sub> lets the LiDAR carry the well-constrained directions, and the heading read-out of the orientation tensor channel gave the largest single gain (Long Corridor 4.53 to 1.98 m).

The error of a switching system follows the share of time handed to VINS-Mono (Spearman -0.95 over 15 detection rules), not the detection quality, which is why the method weights instead of switching.

Without loop closure, F35 gave 0.54 / 1.01 m on Multi Floor, 2.10 / 3.73 m on Long Corridor and 0.29 / 0.56 m on the farm, below Switch-SLAM's 1.61 / 3.63, 2.42 / 5.09 and 0.38 / 1.10 m, each from one run.
This comparison with Switch-SLAM is not like for like: Switch-SLAM uses a LiDAR-inertial front end with an IMU-propagated guess, A-LOAM has no IMU, and the published values are means of three runs.
On GEODE F35 gave 3.26 to 6.36 m and was significantly better than VINS-Mono alone (153 to 272 m, p = 0.008); against F24 it was lower in 11 of 12 pairs, not significantly (p = 0.057).

F26 decided the status from our own channels instead of the published thresholds. It gave similar results to F35 on Long Corridor, GEODE and the farm and higher ones on Multi Floor (0.66 and 0.80 against 0.54 m) and Corridor02 (2.82 against 1.99 m), so the published thresholds added something on those two sequences.

The status guess lowered the error where VINS-Mono starts late or fails. Against F24, F35 was lower on GEODE, Cave02 and the farm and level on Multi Floor and Long Corridor, and Corridor02 was higher by about 0.5 m. On Cave02 F35 gives 6.23 m against 4.4 m for the earlier F8 and F16 versions, and all results are development results.

The next step is a held-out test on a sequence that played no part in the design, with three or more runs each of F35 and F24 and the reading rule written first. A rule for choosing between the fused output and A-LOAM's own mapped pose, which was lower on Long Corridor and Corridor02, and the reason for the Cave02 difference are the open points. Three extensions follow. The first is IMU preintegration in A-LOAM's initial guess; a gyro rotation prior is a cheaper first step, but it gave mixed results when tried in the Switch-SLAM replica, so it needs a proper test. The second is loop closure on every sequence, which was run here only offline on some recordings. The third is the Switch-SLAM replica on Corridor02, Cave02 and GEODE, where it was not run, using a replica version chosen first by a rule written beforehand.<pb/>
